title: India Issues Over 1,300 Commercial Pilot Licences in First Half of 2026, With 41% Trained Abroad
excerpt: The data highlights India's growing reliance on overseas flight schools as domestic training infrastructure struggles to keep pace with the world's fastest-growing aviation market.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India issued 1,331 commercial pilot licences in H1 2026, with 41% trained abroad.
  • CPL issuances have surged 2.5 times since 2018, from 640 to 1,331.
  • Domestic training faces bottlenecks, pushing pilots to train in the US, Australia, and New Zealand.
  • A new Multi-Crew Pilot Licence pathway is under consideration to ease pilot shortages.
  • India needs 30,000 additional pilots in the next decade to support aviation growth.

Data from DGCA and Livemint
  • India's DGCA issued 1,331 commercial pilot licences (CPLs) in the first half of 2026, with 41% of recipients trained at overseas flight schools.
  • The number maintains the trajectory set by record issuances of 1,628 CPLs in 2024, up from just 640 in 2018 — a 2.5x increase in eight years.
  • Domestic training bottlenecks — instructor shortages, spare parts delays and long check-flight wait times — continue to push aspiring pilots toward the US, Australia and New Zealand.
  • A government panel is considering a new Multi-Crew Pilot Licence pathway that would shift more training into simulators to ease the pilot shortage.
https://x.com/IndiaAbroad_/status/2079225649785459133

The Numbers

India issued 1,331 commercial pilot licences in the first six months of 2026, according to Livemint, with a striking 41% of new licence holders having completed their flight training abroad. The figure puts the country on track to match or exceed the record 1,628 CPLs issued in all of 2024, reflecting the aviation sector's continued expansion.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=A-6NuFN9fYI

"In India, it takes double the time," said Hemanth DP, CEO of Asia Pacific Flight Training Academy, in earlier industry commentary."

> **"In India, it takes double the time," said Hemanth DP, CEO of Asia Pacific Flight Training Academy, in earlier industry commentary."**

The growth trajectory has been steep. CPL issuances have increased 2.5 times over the last eight years, from 640 in 2018 to the current pace, driven by India's rapidly expanding airline fleets and the government's "Train in India, Fly in India" push.

Why So Many Train Abroad

The 41% overseas training figure reflects persistent bottlenecks in India's domestic flight training infrastructure. Aviation industry executives point to several factors: a shortage of qualified instructors, disruptions in aviation gasoline supply, spare parts delays and a check-flight process that takes 8-10 months — more than double the time required in the US or Europe.

"It takes around a year to complete CPL training in the West. In India, it takes double the time," said Hemanth DP, CEO of Asia Pacific Flight Training Academy, in earlier industry commentary. "India can actually cater to local demand and even foreign countries by adopting deregulation and best global practices."

The most popular overseas destinations for Indian pilot trainees are the United States, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. Training abroad typically costs ₹55 lakh to ₹1 crore ($65,000-$120,000), with candidates returning to India for DGCA licence conversion — a process that requires additional examinations and verifications.

Challenges in Domestic Training
›Instructor shortages delay training.
›Spare parts delays affect operations.
›Check-flight wait times exceed 8-10 months.
›Training abroad costs ₹55 lakh to ₹1 crore.

Government Response

Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu has acknowledged the training gap while highlighting policy reforms. Six new Flight Training Organisations have been permitted in the last 18 months, with six more in the pipeline. The government has liberalised FTO policy, abolished airport royalties for training operations and rationalised land rentals. DGCA has also digitised the CPL examination process.

Perhaps the most significant reform under consideration is a new Multi-Crew Pilot Licence (MPL) pathway, detailed in a draft report reviewed by Reuters. The proposal would reduce minimum real-aircraft flying hours from 200 to 100-120, with remaining practical training conducted in commercial jet simulators — a model already adopted across Europe, Asia and the Middle East.

"If implemented with strong regulatory oversight and industry collaboration, the new licensing route can reduce manpower shortages."

— Government panel draft report on MPL implementation
Future of Pilot Training
›30,000 pilots needed in the next decade.
›New MPL pathway could reduce flying hours.
›Six new Flight Training Organisations approved.
›Major airlines offer cadet programmes.

The Bigger Picture

India needs an estimated 30,000 additional pilots over the next decade to support its aviation growth. The country's airlines — led by IndiGo, Air India and Akasa Air — are on an aggressive fleet expansion that demands a steady pipeline of trained cockpit crew. Cadet programmes offered by major carriers now cover Type Rating costs in exchange for multi-year service bonds, reducing the financial barrier for new pilots.

For the Indian diaspora, the pilot training pipeline represents both a career opportunity and an immigration story. Thousands of young Indians travel abroad specifically for flight training, creating a community of aviation professionals whose careers straddle borders. Whether India can build domestic capacity fast enough to bring that training home remains one of the aviation sector's most consequential questions.
nri_angle: Many aspiring Indian pilots train in the US, Australia and New Zealand, making this a direct diaspora story about career mobility, immigration pathways and the reverse brain-drain potential in Indian aviation.
